Breath depth — TV as % of FEV1

Tidal volume expressed as a percentage of FEV1 (6.02 L). The endurance breathing target is the 75–85% band (shaded). Higher = the athlete is using more of their available capacity per breath, which lets them hit the same VE at a lower RR — the "deep / slow" pattern. Dylan's headroom is large (FVC = 7.55 L) so there's plenty of structural room to grow.

Reading the chart: Both tests track together through the warm-up range (125 – 175 W) at 36 – 46%. They diverge sharply from 200 W upward.

At 200 W: Dec spikes to 60% briefly then crashes back. May tracks more smoothly at 47%, but ramps cleanly from there. The Dec 200 W spike followed by the 225 W drop back to 47% is a one-off "big breath" not part of a sustained pattern.

At 250 W: Dec sits at 50%, May reaches 67% — climbing into the lower end of the target zone. May's curve is monotonically increasing, which is what you want — every step deeper than the last.

Pattern difference: Dec's 200 W spike-and-drop suggests inconsistent breath control under load. May shows a steady upward staircase — that's the hallmark of trained respiratory drive.

The diagnostic test: watch this through the recovery series. If TV/FEV1 at top step drops back toward 50% as substrate selection returns to Dec baseline, this was a downstream effect of recovery-state physiology. If it stays elevated, then there's an independent breathing-pattern shift worth investigating separately.

Lower HR vs baseline 4 days post-ultra is a clean positive recovery signal. Classic acute post-endurance fatigue patterns (cardiovascular drift, dehydration carry-over, elevated sympathetic tone) would push HR UP at matched watts — May shows the opposite.

What's likely driving the lower HR:
(1) Plasma volume expansion — endurance events trigger durable plasma volume increases (10–15%) that persist for 1–3 weeks. Higher stroke volume → lower HR at the same workload.
(2) Vagal rebound — parasympathetic tone often rises above baseline in the days after a hard event as the body deliberately downshifts.

Expected trajectory: some of this advantage will fade as plasma volume normalizes and vagal tone settles back to baseline. Watch HR at 200 W (Dec 130 → May Day-4 123) across the series. If it stays low through Day-12/16, that's a useful adaptation that persisted. If it drifts back toward 130, that's the transient post-event advantage washing out.

▼ What may have caused this — Fat oxidation dropped across the matched range −19 to −51% at 125-250 W

The flip side of the CHO rise — same recovery signal viewed from the fat side. Dec is true baseline; May Day-4 is the metabolic state 4 days into post-ultra recovery.

What's driving the suppression: two mechanisms operating together.

(1) Glycogen abundance from supercompensation means the body has no need to recruit fat — carbs are everywhere, the engine uses them.
(2) Mitochondrial β-oxidation enzymes remain temporarily downregulated after prolonged endurance work. These enzymes (CPT-1, β-HAD, etc.) take 5–14 days to fully return. So even if the body wanted to burn more fat at moderate watts, the cellular machinery is operating at reduced capacity.

Expected trajectory: fat ox at matched watts should climb back toward Dec baseline as both mechanisms resolve. Most useful step to track is 200 W:

  • 200 W fat ox: Dec 64 g/hr → May Day-4 was 44 g/hr. Watch for return to ~60 g/hr range.
  • 250 W fat ox: Dec 60 g/hr → May Day-4 was 29 g/hr. Slower recovery expected here since it's closer to crossover.

Subjective-feeling correlation worth probing: athletes often report "endurance feels back" before metabolic markers fully return to baseline, or vice versa. Both are valid recovery signals — they just measure different aspects of recovery (perceived effort & motivation vs cellular substrate machinery). Dylan's mismatch (if any) becomes useful self-knowledge for future race prep.

RER is the cleanest single-number recovery signal in the test. It integrates the fat-ox and CHO-ox shifts into one value that tracks substrate selection.

Dec baseline RER curve: 0.77 → 0.84 across 125 → 250 W. Gradual carb engagement.
May Day-4 RER curve: 0.83 → 0.94 across the same range. Already in carb-dominant territory at warm-up wattages.

Why high RER points to supercompensation rather than depletion: classic post-ultra glycogen depletion would push RER DOWN — body forced onto fat because carbs aren't there. May shows the OPPOSITE. Watch through the series: RER at 200 W is probably the most sensitive matched-watts metric. Dec baseline = 0.77. As Dylan walks back toward baseline through Day-8 / Day-12 / Day-16, expect RER at 200 W to drop from May Day-4's 0.87 back toward 0.77. The day it lands near 0.78–0.80 at 200 W, his substrate metabolism is essentially recovered.

Neither test reached RER 1.0 (which marks VT2 / heavy lactate buffering), so this protocol stays submax in both states. Good — that keeps each test light enough not to disturb the recovery process.

Your notes / comments on this metric

VE / VO₂ — VT1 marker (nadir analysis)

VE/VO₂ falls as the aerobic system warms up, hits its nadir at VT1, then rises. The wattage at the nadir is the aerobic threshold (VT1). Reading the curve's slope alone misses this — the nadir point is the diagnostic.

▼ What may have caused this — VT1 unchanged — nadir Dec 195 W → May 197 W Δ +1 W

VT1 has held. The VE/VO₂ nadir is at essentially the same wattage in both tests (Dec 195 W, value 18.59 → May 197 W, value 20.91). The aerobic threshold is preserved 4 days post-ultra.

Why this matters: VT1 is the floor of the aerobic engine — the wattage at which fat-burning is still dominant and ventilatory cost stays low. The fact that it's anchored at ~195–200 W in both tests means Dylan's aerobic base is intact. The fat-ox suppression at matched watts we see in the substrate charts is happening DESPITE an intact VT1 — that's a substrate-recruitment issue (glycogen flooding the system), not a loss of aerobic capacity.

Value of the nadir rose slightly (18.6 → 20.9). This is the elevated CO₂ load from carb-heavy burning pushing the whole curve up — but the WATTAGE at which the curve bottoms hasn't moved. Position, not magnitude, is the threshold.

What to watch: VT1 staying anchored at ~195–200 W across Day-8 / 12 / 16 confirms the aerobic base is durably stable. If it drifts, that's a separate signal worth investigating.

Your notes / comments on this metric

VE / VCO₂ — VT2 marker (nadir analysis)

VE/VCO₂ falls through the moderate-intensity zone, hits its nadir at VT2, then rises as buffering kicks in. The wattage at the nadir is the respiratory compensation point / lactate threshold proxy.

▼ What may have caused this — VT2 has shifted LEFT — nadir Dec 269 W → May 229 W Δ -41 W

VT2 has dropped ~41 W. The VE/VCO₂ nadir sat at Dec 269 W; at May Day-4 it's at 229 W. The respiratory compensation point has moved leftward by a substantial margin.

This is the most important finding in the comparison. Unlike VT1 (which is anchored to aerobic base), VT2 reflects the wattage at which buffering / anaerobic contribution becomes meaningful. It's the ceiling of sustainable work. A 40 W leftward shift in VT2 means the same wattage now produces meaningfully more anaerobic stress than it did at Dec baseline.

Likely driver — recovery state: with mitochondrial respiratory chain capacity temporarily reduced post-ultra, the aerobic ceiling drops while the aerobic floor (VT1) holds. Carbs flood in to compensate at moderate watts, but at higher watts the system can't keep up oxidatively and switches to buffering earlier. So fat-ox loss at moderate watts AND VT2 dropping at high watts are two views of the same underlying recovery state — reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity.

Sustainability picture: what feels "endurance" at Dec baseline now feels "tempo" or "threshold" at Day-4 — because the watts that used to sit below VT2 now sit near or above it. That's the physiological basis for why training the same wattage feels harder right after a big race.

Recovery target: watch VE/VCO₂ nadir position across the series. When it walks back from 229 W toward 269 W, Dylan's ceiling is back. This is probably the metric that should drive when he can return to threshold/tempo work — not how he feels, since feel and metabolism don't always align.

▼ What may have caused this — Alveolar VE rose alongside VE +10 to +20%

Same driver as VE rise. Alveolar VE = (TV − 150 mL dead space) × RR. It's the portion of total VE that actually reaches the alveoli for gas exchange. Since both VE and TV are up, alveolar VE follows.

The gap between total VE and alveolar VE represents dead-space ventilation — air moved but not exchanged. With deeper breaths (higher TV), more of each breath is alveolar and less is dead-space. So even though both rose, May is moving a higher proportion of usable air per breath.

Interpretation — recovery-tracking framing

WHAT THIS COMPARISON IS

Dec 2025 = Dylan's true baseline metabolic state. May 21, 2026 = Dylan 4 days into recovery from the Buckshot 20-hour ultra. Same breakfast both tests; same protocol; same equipment. This is test #1 in a Day-0, Day-4, Day-8, Day-12, Day-16 recovery series designed to map his individual post-ultra recovery curve and correlate it to his subjective feelings.

THE KEY THRESHOLD FINDING — VT1 HELD, VT2 DROPPED

  • VT1 (VE/VO₂ nadir): Dec 195 W → May Day-4 197 W. Unchanged. Aerobic base is intact.
  • VT2 (VE/VCO₂ nadir): Dec 269 W → May Day-4 229 W. Dropped ~40 W. Respiratory compensation point has moved left substantially.
  • This split is diagnostic. VT1 anchored to the aerobic floor, VT2 dropped at the ceiling = mitochondrial respiratory-chain capacity is temporarily reduced. The aerobic base survived the ultra; the ceiling has come down.
  • Practical implication: what was "endurance" at Dec baseline now sits closer to threshold. Workouts at matched watts will feel disproportionately harder than the wattage suggests.

SUBSTRATE — RECOVERY-STATE SIGNATURE

  • RER: 0.84 → 0.94 at top step. CHO ox doubled, fat ox dropped ~50%. Crossover shifted ~90 W left.
  • This is the post-ultra carb-supercompensation pattern, NOT depletion. Glycogen is abundant (RER up, not down) and the body is preferentially burning carbs because (a) glycogen is plentiful, (b) mitochondrial β-oxidation enzymes are still recovering.
  • Substrate finding and VT2 finding are coherent: both point to reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity 4 days post-event. They will recover together.

CARDIOVASCULAR — POSITIVE RECOVERY SIGNAL

  • HR at matched watts LOWER by 4–7 bpm. Consistent with post-event plasma volume expansion and vagal rebound — well-documented post-endurance physiology that fades over 1–3 weeks.
  • Confirms this is recovery-state, not depletion: fatigue/depletion would raise HR, not lower it.

WHAT TO WATCH IN THE NEXT TESTS

  • VE/VCO₂ nadir wattage — the most actionable single metric. Currently at 229 W; recovery target 269 W. When it walks back, his ceiling is back.
  • VE/VO₂ nadir wattage — should stay anchored near 195 W. Drift here would signal aerobic base disturbance, which would be concerning.
  • RER at 200 W — currently 0.87, target 0.78 (Dec baseline).
  • Fat ox at 200 W — currently 44 g/hr, target ~60 g/hr.
  • HR at 200 W — currently 123, was 130 in Dec. If it stays low, plasma volume gain stuck; if it drifts back, transient.
  • Dylan's subjective "feel" log — most interesting question is whether his "I feel back" report aligns with the VT2 wattage returning or with the substrate normalizing. They may diverge.

NO TRAINING PRESCRIPTION CHANGES YET

The VT2 shift specifically argues for keeping training intensity LOW until the ceiling returns. Working at wattages that sit above the depressed VT2 will be much more anaerobically stressful than the same wattages were pre-ultra, even though they feel familiar. Wait for the Day-8 / Day-12 trajectory before prescribing intensity work.
